sources.title: Human History Map research coverage registry

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 BCE borders
sources.note: First exact target geometry: three parts spanning a very broad southern boreal and transitional belt.

sources.title: Human History Map 1000 BCE borders
sources.note: Second observed interval and an exactly coordinate-identical target geometry.

sources.title: Human History Map 700 BCE borders
sources.note: Third observed interval and another exactly coordinate-identical target geometry.

sources.title: Human History Map 500 BCE borders
sources.note: Island components disappear while the giant mainland component remains.

sources.title: Human History Map 400 BCE borders
sources.note: Copied mainland geometry continues across the fifth observed interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 323 BCE borders
sources.note: Small coordinate drift creates a new hash without changing tested point membership.

sources.title: Human History Map 300 BCE borders
sources.note: The 323 BCE mainland geometry is copied into the next interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 200 BCE borders
sources.note: The same broad mainland geometry continues for another interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 100 BCE borders
sources.note: Southern edge contracts and tested points at The Pas and Quebec City leave the target.

sources.title: Human History Map 1 BCE borders
sources.note: One-year coordinate variant at the BCE to CE seam.

sources.title: Human History Map 100 CE borders
sources.note: Broad single polygon returns to the earlier 420-position geometry.

sources.title: Human History Map 200 CE borders
sources.note: Copied broad geometry for the 200 to 300 CE interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 300 CE borders
sources.note: Copied broad geometry for the 300 to 400 CE interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 400 CE borders
sources.note: Copied broad geometry for the 400 to 500 CE interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 500 CE borders
sources.note: A coordinate revision retains the same sampled regional membership.

sources.title: Human History Map 600 CE borders
sources.note: Earlier wider southern geometry returns at the start of this interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 700 CE borders
sources.note: The 600 CE geometry is copied through the next century.

sources.title: Human History Map 800 CE borders
sources.note: Major contraction removes Alaska and Yukon and limits the target to southern and central Canada.

sources.title: Human History Map 900 CE borders
sources.note: The sharply contracted 800 CE geometry is copied.

sources.title: Human History Map 1000 CE borders
sources.note: Small northward and eastward edits change positions and bounds.

sources.title: Human History Map 1100 CE borders
sources.note: A revised 105-position polygon begins another copied sequence.

sources.title: Human History Map 1200 CE borders
sources.note: The 1100 CE target geometry is repeated exactly here.

sources.title: Human History Map 1279 CE borders
sources.note: Coordinate drift creates a new hash while the overall footprint stays similar.

sources.title: Human History Map 1300 CE borders
sources.note: The 1279 geometry is copied into the next interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 1400 CE borders
sources.note: Final pre-gap polygon with another small coordinate revision.

sources.title: Human History Map 1492 CE borders
sources.note: Target absent during the 1492 to 1500 coverage gap amid overlapping modern-name overlays.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 CE borders
sources.note: Target returns as a smaller polygon from Alberta and Saskatchewan to Labrador.

sources.title: Human History Map 1530 CE borders
sources.note: Target collapses into four coarse fragments, including one seven-point western polygon.

sources.title: Human History Map 1600 CE borders
sources.note: Two simultaneous exact-id features appear, one western and one reaching the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence.

sources.title: Human History Map 1650 CE borders
sources.note: Only the coarse seven-point western target feature remains here.

sources.title: Human History Map 1700 CE borders
sources.note: The western remnant receives a slight coordinate revision here.

sources.title: Human History Map 1715 CE borders
sources.note: The revised western remnant is copied through the final observed interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 1783 CE borders
sources.note: Target disappears into a colonial sovereignty redraw dominated by Rupert's Land.

sources.title: Hare and colleagues, Ethnographic and Archaeological Investigations of Alpine Ice Patches
sources.note: Dated Yukon hunting weapons, rare organic preservation, method, community partnership and limits on campsite inference.

sources.title: Parks Canada, Yukon Ice Patches
sources.note: Institutional synthesis of 7,500 years of caribou hunting, perishable artifacts and First Nations research collaboration.

sources.title: Diane K. Hanson, Archaeological Investigations at the Ringling Site
sources.note: Excavated hearths and worked copper, metallographic support for annealing and uncertainty over object function.

sources.title: Simeone and Miller, Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias Ethnographic Overview
sources.note: Named later Ahtna seasonal practices and colonial disruptions used only as localized comparison.

sources.title: National Park Service, Kijik Archeological District
sources.note: Dena'ina settlement remains, caches, steam baths, later disease and continued community return.

sources.title: Reger and Mobley, Dena'ina Use of Marine Resources for Food and Tools
sources.note: Regional archaeological evidence for shell containers, tools, raw materials and coastal food use.

sources.title: Karen K. Gaul, Nanutset: An Ethnohistory of Lake Clark
sources.note: Historically recorded Dena'ina household, cooking and healing knowledge, clearly later than most atlas intervals.

sources.title: Prince of Wales Northern Heritage Centre, This Land Is Our Home: Fishing
sources.note: Named Yellowknives Dene testimony and a willow-bark fish net as a later material comparison.

sources.title: Prince of Wales Northern Heritage Centre, This Land Is Our Home: Sewing
sources.note: Named maker and family memory for a caribou-skin coat designed for warmth, pregnancy and childcare.

sources.title: James Morrison, Notes on Algonquin Material Culture
sources.note: Later localized descriptions of portable lodges, snowshoe variation, containers and seasonal work.

sources.title: James Morrison, Algonquin History in the Ottawa River Watershed
sources.note: Watershed archaeology, native copper, long-distance materials, place knowledge and attribution cautions.

sources.title: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage, Precontact Beothuk Land Use
sources.note: Localized Newfoundland evidence and reconstruction of coast-to-interior seasonal land use.

sources.title: Ralph T. Pastore, The Boyd's Cove Beothuk Site
sources.note: Excavated house pits, preservation conditions, varied fauna, hearths and contextual interpretation.

sources.title: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage, Beothuk Hunting and Food Preparation
sources.note: Specific tools, drying, smoking, hot-stone cooking and storage practices from archaeological and historical evidence.

sources.title: Ralph T. Pastore, Beothuk Culture
sources.note: Regional evidence for houses, tools, ochre, beliefs and historically recorded daily life.

sources.title: Ralph T. Pastore, Post-Contact Beothuk History
sources.note: European encroachment, resource restriction, encounters and the limits of colonial written accounts.

sources.title: Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage, Disappearance of the Beothuk
sources.note: Evidence and uncertainty around colonial violence, disease, population loss and Beothuk survival.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw Cree Cultural Institute, Ubagaan
sources.note: Nineteenth-century Mistissini toboggans and living terminology used as later comparison.

sources.title: Grand Council of the Crees, Annual Report 2013 to 2014
sources.note: Child-sized Waskaganish snowshoes and ongoing making and use, not an ancient dated find.

sources.title: Aanischaaukamikw, Adelyna Sara Snow's Walking Out Ceremony
sources.note: A named modern child, family-made clothing and a living ceremony used only as comparison.

sources.title: Parks Canada, York Factory National Historic Site
sources.note: Institutional history of a major fur-trade post and the Indigenous relationships surrounding it.

sources.title: Canadian Museum of History, Gwich'in Snowshoes
sources.note: Collaborative museum record for snowshoe materials, use, ochre and later oral testimony.

sources.title: Government of Ontario, Ecosystems of Ontario: Ecozones and Ecoregions
sources.note: Official environmental synthesis distinguishing boreal, Great Lakes and other ecological zones.

sources.title: Roland Bohr, Aboriginal Archery in the Central Subarctic and Eastern Woodlands
sources.note: Regional archaeological synthesis of bows, arrows, hunting, warfare and preservation limits.

sources.title: Karl Reinhard, Archaeoparasitology in North America
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review of coprolites, skeletons, latrine soils, parasite evidence and identification limits.

sources.title: Parks Canada, People of the Lakes: Vuntut National Park
sources.note: Named Gwich'in seasonal foods, travel and continuing land use used as later regional comparison.

sources.title: Canadian Museum of History, Fur Trade
sources.note: Indigenous transport knowledge, exchange networks and seventeenth- and eighteenth-century trade relationships.

sources.title: Algonquian Dictionaries Project, Language and Dialect
sources.note: Modern linguistic explanation of distinct Cree varieties, useful for rejecting one umbrella language.

sources.title: Government of Ontario, Indigenous Archaeology
sources.note: Official guidance emphasizing Indigenous engagement in archaeological work and care for heritage.

sources.title: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Archaeology in Newfoundland and Labrador 1983
sources.note: Primary excavation report on Boyd's Cove stratigraphy, houses, Little Passage links and interpretive uncertainty.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Atlas umbrella for diverse North American communities, 1500 BCE to 1783 CE.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed id is preserved solely as a historical-basemap display key from 1500 BCE to 1783 CE.
The label is an atlas umbrella, not one people, state, language, economy or archaeological culture.
Thirty-one observed intervals cover the lifetime except for an explicit 1492 to 1500 atlas gap.
The early polygon is a southern, overbroad boreal and transition belt that excludes much of the geographic Subarctic.
The 800 CE contraction, 1530 fragmentation and 1783 redraw are map seams rather than dated cultural events.
The 1600 snapshot has two simultaneous features with the exact same id and radically different footprints.
Direct finds, scientific or experimental inference and later localized comparison remain explicitly distinguished.
No contemporaneous written-language sample is supplied because no script is securely attributable to this category and interval.
The 1783 endpoint is a colonial atlas redraw, not a shared fall; predecessor and successor arrays remain empty.
